summary: Gives functional requirements for carrying multicast traffic over Virtual Private LAN Service. It covers the viewpoints of both end users and service providers, and is meant as guidance for solutions that would be designed later.

plainLanguage.summary: A company network spread across cities should send one video to many viewers efficiently. This note lists what customers and providers need from such a service before anyone builds it.

subtitle: Guidelines for efficient multicast delivery across virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) floods all multicast and broadcast frames to every member site, wasting bandwidth when sites have no interested receivers. Additionally, when multiple pseudowires share the same physical link, multicast replication creates redundant copies over that link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines functional requirements for optimizing multicast in VPLS from both customer and service provider perspectives, including membership tracking, efficient distribution tunnels, and security controls.
tldr.outcome: Solutions following these requirements enable service providers to deploy multicast services like IPTV and multicast IP VPNs while scaling to larger VPLS networks with many sites.

facts.label: Bandwidth waste
facts.value: 20 PEs with 50 Mbps input = 1000 Mbps on one shared link

today: RFC 5501 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It serves as a requirements baseline for solutions such as the BGP-MVPN (Multicast VPN) architecture and VPLS optimizations that followed.

sections.title: Overview of VPLS and Multicast Challenges
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) creates a multipoint-to-multipoint Ethernet VPN by connecting customer LAN segments across a provider backbone. Unlike point-to-point connections, VPLS forwards traffic based on MAC address learning, emulating a provider-managed bridge.

The original VPLS design handles multicast and broadcast by replicating frames to all sites in the service. This approach has two major scalability problems. First, multicast traffic reaches sites with no interested receivers, consuming bandwidth and provider resources (Issue A). Second, when multiple replicated copies traverse the same physical link between provider routers, bandwidth is wasted on redundancy (Issue B). As multicast applications such as IPTV grow in popularity, these inefficiencies become critical.
sections.plainLanguage: VPLS works like a bridge that connects several offices over a network. Right now, when one office broadcasts something, it goes to every other office, even ones that do not want it. That is wasteful.

sections.title: Key Concepts: Multicast Domain and Distribution Tunnels
sections.content:
A multicast domain defines the area in which multicast data is transmitted. In VPLS, this can be a VLAN within the customer network or a scope defined by IP multicast membership (join groups). A solution should prevent multicast from flooding unnecessarily outside the domain and ensure the domain size matches customer Layer-3 multicast needs.

An MDTunnel (Multicast Distribution Tunnel) is a path through the provider network carrying customer multicast traffic. It can be point-to-point (traditional unicast pseudowire replication), point-to-multipoint (reaching multiple sites directly), or multipoint-to-multipoint. Solutions may use different tunneling technologies such as P2MP-LSP (Label Switched Path) or multicast IP trees.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast domain is like a group of people who want the same video. An MDTunnel is the path the video takes across the provider network to reach them.

sections.title: Customer-Side Requirements
sections.content:
Customers expect multicast over VPLS to behave like a native Ethernet LAN. Solutions MUST allow Layer-2 Ethernet control protocols (such as Spanning Tree) to work transparently. They MAY examine Layer-3 multicast protocols (PIM, IGMP, MLD) to optimize forwarding, but MUST NOT require customers to change their protocol configuration.

Customers require quality of service at least equivalent to unicast traffic, with separate QoS treatment for multicast and unicast to prevent multicast from starving other services. Solutions SHOULD provide SLA parameter measurement (statistics per multicast group, one-way delay, jitter, group join/leave delay) and MUST support policing to limit multicast traffic per customer.

For high-availability networks, multicast forwarding restoration time MUST NOT exceed the failure detection timer of customer routing protocols (typically 105 seconds for PIM). Customers may also require fate-sharing between unicast and multicast connectivity, where if either fails, the other is disabled simultaneously.
sections.plainLanguage: Customers want multicast to work like a real Ethernet network. They need good quality, the network should not let one customer's multicast break everyone else's connection, and if the network breaks, it should break for both regular traffic and multicast together.

sections.title: Provider Network Requirements: Scalability and Security
sections.content:
Service providers must scale multicast to an increasing number of PEs (Provider Edges), VPLS instances, sites per instance, VLANs, MAC groups, and IP multicast channels. A solution MUST document its scalability characteristics quantitatively: how much state a PE device consumes, how much control-plane bandwidth is needed for signaling, and how the solution handles growing numbers of multicast groups.

Because customers may be untrusted, providers face security threats. A malicious customer can launch a denial-of-service attack by joining too many groups, sending malformed control packets, or flooding with high-volume multicast data. Solutions SHOULD protect the provider network by enforcing limits on multicast state per customer VPN, filtering invalid multicast addresses, and supporting rate-limiting of both control packets and data traffic.

Solutions MUST provide operational tools for testing multicast connectivity, verifying membership information, monitoring multicast traffic statistics, and detecting and isolating faults. Mechanisms for dynamic multicast membership discovery at the PE level help keep the control plane light and reduce configuration overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers need to know their network can handle many customers and many groups. They also need to protect themselves from bad customers who might break things on purpose, and they need tools to find and fix problems when multicast does not work.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
A fundamental trade-off exists between optimality (bandwidth efficiency) and state resource consumption (memory and CPU needed to track multicast). Solving Issue A (replication to non-member sites) requires PEs to maintain per-group membership information, consuming resources. Solving Issue B (replication on shared links) may require P routers to maintain tree topology information.

Solutions do not need to optimize both issues equally. A solution SHOULD identify which issue(s) it targets and provide metrics to evaluate how well it performs. Some solutions may prioritize bandwidth optimization and accept higher state resource usage, while others may accept less optimality to minimize router overhead.

Solutions SHOULD support both static multicast topology configuration (where administrators define groups and reachability) and dynamic membership tracking (where the network learns groups from customer signaling). Backward compatibility with existing VPLS deployments is important: a common VPLS instance should be able to contain both PEs that support multicast optimization and those that do not, with optimization benefits realized only between compliant PEs.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a trade-off between saving bandwidth and using less computer power. Solutions can pick which problem to solve first. Ideally, solutions should work with old networks that do not have multicast optimization.

sections.title: Security Threat Analysis
sections.content:
Five major threat classes affect multicast VPLS. First, a customer can join excessive multicast groups or send high-rate control packets, exhausting PE resources. Second, malformed or spoofed control packets may corrupt a PE. Third, rapid state changes in multicast membership can overwhelm the control plane. Fourth, high-volume multicast or broadcast data traffic can exhaust link bandwidth. Fifth, large volumes of unknown-destination unicast frames, which must be flooded in VPLS, can saturate the network.

Provider defenses include configurable per-VPN state resource limits (not per-provider limits, to isolate the damage from one malicious customer), traffic policing by type (multicast, broadcast, and unicast controlled separately), and dampening mechanisms that throttle rapid multicast state changes. Since L2VPN typically lacks Layer-3 authentication at the PE-CE boundary, implementations should apply conservative validation to customer control packets and filter against invalid MAC and IP multicast addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad customers can cause problems by sending too many groups, breaking packets, changing things too fast, or sending huge amounts of traffic. Providers protect themselves with rules that limit one customer's damage and with checks to reject bad packets.

items.title: Issue A
items.text: Multicast floods to all sites, even those with no interested receivers, wasting bandwidth and resources.

items.title: Issue B
items.text: Multiple copies of the same multicast traverse shared physical links between routers, duplicating bandwidth waste.

viz.caption: Where multicast protocols operate in VPLS

layers.label: Customer routers and applications
layers.detail: Run IP multicast protocols (PIM, IGMP, MLD) and multicast applications.

layers.label: VPLS layer
layers.detail: Transparently carries customer Layer 2 and Layer 3 multicast traffic.

layers.label: Provider backbone
layers.detail: Uses distribution tunnels (P2MP-LSP, multicast IP trees) to optimize replication across sites.
